notes.heading: The mole and Avogadro constant
points: The mole (mol) is the SI unit for amount of substance.
One mole is exactly 6.02214076 × 10^23 elementary entities; this count is the Avogadro constant, N_A.
N_A has units mol–1. Number of particles N = n × N_A.
Entities can be atoms, molecules, ions, electrons or other particles; always state which entity you mean (e.g. 1 mol of O atoms vs O2).

notes.heading: Relative atomic and formula mass
points: Ar compares an atom's mass with one-twelfth of a carbon-12 atom's mass. Mr does the same for a molecule or formula unit.
Both are ratios, so they have no units.
Add the Ar values of all atoms in the formula; ionic compounds use the smallest formula unit, e.g. CaCl2 = 40.08 + 2 × 35.45 = 110.98.
For hydrates add water as a unit: CuSO4•5H2O includes 5 × Mr(H2O), giving 249.72.
Use the Ar values from the data booklet to two decimals; never round Mr to a whole number.

notes.heading: Molar mass and n = m/M
points: Molar mass M is the mass of one mole, in g mol–1. It is numerically equal to Ar or Mr.
Use n = m/M, with n in mol, m in g and M in g mol–1 (this relationship is in the data booklet).
To count atoms: find n of the compound, multiply by atoms per formula unit, then multiply by N_A.
Example: 2.80 g sucrose (M = 342.34) is 0.00818 mol and contains 11 times that amount of O atoms.

notes.heading: Empirical and molecular formulae
points: Empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms; molecular formula gives the actual atoms per molecule. Ionic compounds use the empirical formula.
The empirical formula also shows the mole ratio of the elements.
Percentage to formula: take 100 g, so % becomes grams; divide by Ar to get moles; divide by the smallest; multiply to reach whole numbers.
Combustion analysis: all C ends up in CO2 (n(C) = n(CO2)) and all H in H2O (n(H) = 2 × n(H2O)).
Molecular formula: divide the molar mass by the empirical formula mass to get a whole-number multiplier, then multiply the empirical formula by it.
Percentage composition: mass of element in one mole ÷ molar mass × 100%.

notes.heading: Concentration of solutions
points: Molar concentration [X] = n/V, with V in dm3 (n = CV is in the data booklet). Units mol dm–3; 1 dm3 = 1000 cm3.
Square brackets mean the concentration of that specific species, e.g. [Cl–].
Mass concentration in g dm–3 = mass/volume. Convert using ρ = c × M, or c = ρ/M.
Dilution keeps the moles of solute unchanged, so c1V1 = c2V2.
Convert cm3 to dm3 by dividing by 1000 before substituting.

notes.heading: Avogadro's law and gas volumes
points: Equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure hold equal numbers of molecules.
So the amount of gas is proportional to volume: n1/n2 = V1/V2.
For gases measured under the same conditions, volume ratios equal the coefficient ratios in the balanced equation, so moles need not be found.
It applies only to gases, not to liquids or solids such as liquid water in an equation.

definitions.definition: The SI unit of amount of substance; one mole contains exactly 6.02214076 × 10^23 elementary entities, the Avogadro constant.
must_say: SI unit of amount of substance
definitions.trap: Saying a mole is a mass or just 'a number of atoms' without naming the entity.

definitions.definition: The number of elementary entities in one mole, 6.02214076 × 10^23, with units mol–1.
definitions.trap: Leaving off the unit mol–1 or treating it as a unitless number.

definitions.definition: The ratio of the mass of an atom to one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom; it has no units.
definitions.trap: Defining it for an 'element' or giving it units such as g.

definitions.definition: The ratio of the mass of a molecule (or formula unit) to one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
definitions.trap: Examiners report most candidates cannot define it; do not give units or say 'mass of a molecule' only.

definitions.definition: The mass of one mole of a substance, in g mol–1; it is numerically equal to Ar or Mr.
definitions.trap: Mixing it up with relative mass, which has no units.

definitions.definition: The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound.
definitions.trap: Giving the actual number of atoms, which is the molecular formula.

definitions.definition: The actual number of atoms of each element present in one molecule of the compound.
definitions.trap: Forgetting it is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula.

definitions.definition: The amount of solute in moles divided by the volume of the solution in dm3, with units mol dm–3.
definitions.trap: Using the solvent volume instead of the final solution volume, or cm3 instead of dm3.

definitions.definition: Equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules.
definitions.trap: Omitting 'same temperature and pressure' or applying it to liquids and solids.
